claim: Rats trained on a multisensory discrimination task performed better when responding to combined auditory and visual cues compared to trials with only auditory or visual cues.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Chang et al., 2022; Raposo et al., 2014; Angelaki et al., 2009; Smyre et al., 2021), rats performed better when responding to combined auditory and visual cues (multisensory trials) compared to trials with only auditory or visual cue (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1b and references to previous studies.

claim: Reaction time was shorter in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials.
source: Reaction time, measured as the time from cue onset to when the rat left the central port, was shorter in multisensory trials (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reaction time measurements shown in Figures 1c and 1d.

claim: Mean reaction time across rats was 367±53ms for multisensory trials, 426±60ms for auditory trials, and 417±53ms for visual trials.
source: mean reaction time across rats, multisensory, 367±53ms; auditory, 426±60ms; visual, 417±53ms; multisensory vs. each unisensory, p<0.001, paired t-test. Figure 1d
evidence: The claim is supported by specific reaction time measurements with statistical comparison.

claim: 35% of AC neurons showed visual responses during the multisensory discrimination task.
source: Interestingly, a substantial proportion of neurons (35%, 196/559) showed visual responses (Figure 2b)
evidence: The claim is supported by neuronal recording data showing the proportion of visually responsive neurons.

claim: The proportion of AC neurons showing visual responses was significantly higher in the multisensory discrimination group (35%) compared to the free-choice group (14%).
source: which was notably higher than the 14% (14%, 39/275, χ2 = 27.5, p < 0.001) recorded in another group of rats (n=8) engaged in a free-choice task where rats were not required to discriminate triggered cues and could receive water rewards with any behavioral response (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a statistical comparison between two experimental groups using chi-square test.

claim: Multisensory discrimination training enhances visual representation in the auditory cortex.
source: This suggests multisensory discrimination training enhances visual representation in the auditory cortex.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed difference in visual responsiveness between task groups.

claim: 27% of AC neurons responded to both auditory and visual stimuli (audiovisual neurons).
source: Notably, 27% (150/559) of neurons responded to both auditory and visual stimuli (audiovisual neurons)
evidence: The claim is supported by neuronal classification data from recordings.

claim: 61% of auditory-responsive neurons exhibited significant auditory selectivity during the task.
source: We found a significant majority (61%, 307/506) of auditory-responsive neurons exhibited this selectivity during the task (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis of neuronal responses to different auditory cues.

claim: Most auditory-selective neurons favored the high-frequency tone (A10k preferred: 261; A3k preferred: 46).
source: Notably, most neurons favored the high-frequency tone (A10k preferred: 261; A3k preferred: 46, Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by counts of neurons with different auditory preferences.

claim: Neurons in the AC and medial prefrontal cortex selectively preferred the tone associated with the behavioral choice contralateral to the recorded cortices during sound discrimination tasks.
source: This aligns with findings that neurons in the AC and medial prefrontal cortex selectively preferred the tone associated with the behavioral choice contralateral to the recorded cortices during sound discrimination tasks (Chang et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 41% of visually-responsive neurons showed a significant visual preference.
source: Regarding the visual modality, 41% (80/196) of visually-responsive neurons showed a significant visual preference (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis of visual selectivity.

claim: A greater proportion of neurons favored the visual stimulus (Vvt) associated with the contralateral choice, with a 3:1 ratio of Vvt-preferred to Vhz-preferred neurons.
source: Similar to the auditory selectivity observed, a greater proportion of neurons favored the visual stimulus (Vvt) associated with the contralateral choice, with a 3:1 ratio of Vvt-preferred to Vhz-preferred neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of visual preference distribution.

claim: Among audiovisual neurons with significant visual selectivity, the majority favored Vvt (Vvt preferred vs. Vhz preferred, 48 vs 7).
source: Among audiovisual neurons with a significant visual selectivity, the majority favored Vvt (Vvt preferred vs. Vhz preferred, 48 vs 7; Figure 2g)
evidence: The claim is supported by counts of neurons with different visual preferences among audiovisual neurons.

claim: The auditory input acts as a 'teaching signal' that shapes visual processing through selective reinforcement of specific visual pathways during associative learning.
source: We propose that the auditory input, which dominates within the auditory cortex, acts as a 'teaching signal' that shapes visual processing through the selective reinforcement of specific visual pathways during associative learning.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on observed patterns of visual selectivity.

claim: 79% of neurons showing significant multisensory selectivity exhibited a preference for the multisensory cue (A10kVvt) guiding the contralateral choice.
source: Similar to auditory selectivity, the vast majority of neurons (79%, 270/340) showing significant multisensory selectivity exhibited a preference for the multisensory cue (A10kVvt) guiding the contralateral choice (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of multisensory selectivity.

claim: Pairing auditory cues with visual cues significantly improved the neurons' ability to distinguish between auditory stimuli alone.
source: We found that pairing auditory cues with visual cues significantly improved the neurons' ability to distinguish between auditory stimuli alone (mean absolute auditory selectivity: 0.23±0.11; mean absolute multisensory selectivity: 0.25±0.12; p<0.0001, Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test; Figure 2i).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of auditory and multisensory selectivity.

claim: AC neurons reached 90% decoding accuracy approximately 18ms earlier in multisensory trials compared to auditory trials.
source: While decoding accuracy was similar for auditory and multisensory conditions, the presence of visual cues accelerated the decoding process, with AC neurons reaching 90% accuracy approximately 18ms earlier in multisensory trials (Figure 2j)
evidence: The claim is supported by population decoding analysis comparing temporal dynamics.

claim: AC neurons could discriminate between two visual targets with around 80% accuracy.
source: Interestingly, AC neurons could discriminate between two visual targets with around 80% accuracy (Figure 2j)
evidence: The claim is supported by population decoding analysis of visual discrimination.

claim: AC neurons in the free-choice group lacked visual discrimination ability and showed lower accuracy for auditory cues.
source: However, AC neurons in the free-choice group lacked visual discrimination ability and showed lower accuracy for auditory cues (Figure 2k)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of decoding performance between task groups.

claim: Over a third (34%, 192 of 559) of AC neurons displayed significant visual modulation of their auditory responses in one or both audiovisual pairings.
source: Over a third (34%, 192 of 559) of AC neurons displayed significant visual modulation of their auditory responses in one or both audiovisual pairings (p<0.05, permutation test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of multisensory integration.

claim: AC neurons adopted distinct integration strategies depending on the specific auditory-visual pairing presented.
source: Interestingly, AC neurons adopted distinct integration strategies depending on the specific auditory-visual pairing presented.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations of differential multisensory responses across pairings.

claim: Multisensory enhancement was mainly specific to the A10k-Vvt pairing.
source: This enhancement was mainly specific to the A10k-Vvt pairing, as shown by population averages (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by population-level analysis of multisensory integration.

claim: Within the A10k-Vvt pairing, significantly more neurons exhibited enhancement than inhibition (114 vs 36).
source: Within this pairing, significantly more neurons exhibited enhancement than inhibition (114 vs 36) (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by counts of neurons showing different integration patterns.

claim: The A3k-Vhz pairing showed a balanced distribution of enhancement and inhibition (35 vs 33).
source: In contrast, the A3k-Vhz pairing showed a balanced distribution of enhancement and inhibition (35 vs 33; Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by counts of neurons showing different integration patterns.

claim: Mean MSI for the A10k-Vvt pairing was significantly higher than for the A3k-Vhz pairing (0.047±0.124 vs 0.003±0.096; paired t-test, p<0.001).
source: This resulted in a significantly higher mean MSI for the A10k-Vvt pairing compared to the A3k-Vhz pairing (0.047±0.124 vs 0.003±0.096; paired t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of MSI values between pairings.

claim: Among audiovisual neurons, mean MSI was 0.119±0.105 in A10k-Vvt pairing vs. 0.020±0.083 in A3k-Vhz pairing (paired t-test, p<0.00001).
source: Among audiovisual neurons, this biasing is even more pronounced (enhanced vs. inhibited: 62 vs 2 in A10k-Vvt pairing, 6 vs 13 in A3k-Vhz pairing; mean MSI: 0.119±0.105 in A10k-Vvt pairing vs. 0.020±0.083 A3k-Vhz pairing, paired t-test, p<0.00001; Figure 3f).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of MSI in audiovisual neurons.

claim: AC neurons in the free-choice group did not exhibit differential integration patterns.
source: In contrast, AC neurons in the free-choice group did not exhibit differential integration patterns (Figure 3g and h)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of integration patterns between task groups.

claim: There was a significant correlation (R=0.65, p<0.001) between the difference in MSI between A10k-Vvt and A3k-Vhz pairings and the change in neuronal multisensory versus auditory selectivity.
source: We found a significant correlation between these measures (R=0.65, p<0.001, Pearson correlation test).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between MSI difference and selectivity change.

claim: Population neurons could effectively discriminate between multisensory and unisensory stimuli.
source: SVM decoding analysis confirmed that population neurons could effectively discriminate between multisensory and unisensory stimuli (Figure 3i).
evidence: The claim is supported by SVM decoding analysis.

claim: For most neurons, the observed multisensory response approximated 83% of the sum of the auditory and visual responses.
source: Specifically, as exemplified in Figure 3k, the observed multisensory response approximated 83% of the sum of the auditory and visual responses in most cases, as quantified in Figure 3l.
evidence: The claim is supported by bootstrap analysis comparing observed and predicted multisensory responses.

claim: The mean MSI for incorrect choices was significantly lower than that for correct choices in the A10k-Vvt pairing (correct vs. incorrect: 0.059±0.137 vs 0.006±0.207; p=0.005, paired t-test).
source: The mean MSI for incorrect choices was significantly lower than that for correct choices (correct vs. incorrect: 0.059±0.137 vs 0.006±0.207; p=0.005, paired t-test, Figure 4b and c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of MSI between correct and incorrect trials.

claim: The A3k-Vhz pairing showed no difference in MSI between correct and incorrect trials (correct vs. incorrect: 0.011±0.081 vs 0.003±0.199; p=0.542, paired t-test).
source: In contrast, the A3k-Vhz pairing showed no difference in MSI between correct and incorrect trials (correct vs. incorrect: 0.011±0.081 vs 0.003±0.199; p=0.542, paired t-test, Figure 4d and e).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison showing no significant difference.

claim: The unmatched visual cue (Vhz) generally failed to significantly enhance the response to the preferred sound (A10k) in most cases (mean MSI: 0.052±0.097 for A10k-Vvt pairing vs. 0.016±0.123 for A10k-Vhz pairing, p<0.0001, paired t-test).
source: Unlike Vvt, the unmatched visual cue, Vhz, generally failed to significantly enhance the response to the preferred sound (A10k) in most cases (mean MSI: 0.052±0.097 for A10k-Vvt pairing vs. 0.016±0.123 for A10k-Vhz pairing, p<0.0001, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of MSI for matched vs. unmatched pairings.

claim: Neither associative nor non-associative visual cue could boost neurons' response to the nonpreferred sound (A3k) overall (mean MSI: 0.003±0.008 for A3k-Vhz pairing vs. 0.003±0.006 for A3k-Vvt pairing, p=0.19, paired t-test).
source: In contrast, neither associative nor non-associative visual cue could boost neurons' response to the nonpreferred sound (A3k) overall (mean MSI: 0.003±0.008 for A3k-Vhz pairing vs. 0.003±0.006 for A3k-Vvt pairing, p=0.19, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison showing no significant difference.

claim: The population of neurons could effectively discriminate two target multisensory cues.
source: We found that the population of neurons could effectively discriminate two target multisensory cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by decoding analysis of population responses.

claim: Grouped neurons could discriminate matched and unmatched visual cues paired with A3k with a decoding accuracy of 0.79.
source: While matched and unmatched visual cues failed to differentially modulate the response to the nonpreferred sound (A3k) at the single-neuron level, grouped neurons still could discriminate them with a decoding accuracy of 0.79 (Figure 5e)
evidence: The claim is supported by population decoding analysis.

claim: The decoding accuracy for discriminating A10k-Vvt and A10k-Vhz pairings was 0.81.
source: close to the accuracy of 0.81 for discriminating between A10k-Vvt and A10k-Vhz pairings.
evidence: The claim is supported by population decoding analysis.

claim: Most neurons in the right AC preferred the cue directing the contralateral choice, regardless of whether it was auditory or visual.
source: Our data showed that most neurons in the right AC preferred the cue directing the contralateral choice, regardless of whether it was auditory or visual.
evidence: The claim is a summary of observed neuronal preferences in the right AC.

claim: In the left AC, the average response across neurons preferred cues guiding the contralateral choice (A3k, Vhz and A3kVhz).
source: Similar to the right AC, the average response across neurons in the left AC preferred cues guiding the contralateral choice (Figure 6c). However, in this case, the preferred cues are A3k, Vhz and the audiovisual pairing A3kVhz.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of neuronal responses in the left AC.

claim: More auditory-responsive neurons in the left AC favored the sound denoting the contralateral choice.
source: As shown in Figure 6d, more auditory-responsive neurons favored the sound denoting the contralateral choice.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of auditory selectivity in the left AC.

claim: In the left AC, mean MSI in the A3k-Vhz pairing is substantially higher than in the A10k-Vvt pairing among audiovisual neurons (0.135±0.126 to -0.039±0.138; p<0.0001, paired t-test).
source: In audiovisual neurons, mean MSI in the A3k-Vhz pairing is substantially higher than in the A10k-Vvt pairing (0.135±0.126 to -0.039±0.138; p<0.0001, paired t-test; Figure 6g).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of MSI in left AC audiovisual neurons.

claim: 28% of recorded AC neurons in the unisensory training group responded to visual target cues.
source: Among recorded AC neurons, 28% (49/174) responded to visual target cues (Figure 7b).
evidence: The claim is supported by neuronal classification data from the unisensory training group.

claim: Most visually responsive neurons in the unisensory training group lacked a visual preference.
source: Unlike the multisensory training group, most visually responsive neurons in the unisensory training group lacked a visual preference, regardless of whether they were visually-only responsive or audiovisual (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of visual selectivity between training groups.

claim: 47% of recorded neurons in the unisensory training group demonstrated clear auditory discrimination, with most (80%, 60 out of 75) favoring the sound guiding the contralateral choice.
source: Interestingly, similar to the multisensory training group, nearly half of the recorded neurons (47%, 75/159) demonstrated clear auditory discrimination, with most (80%, 60 out of 75) favoring the sound guiding the contralateral choice (Figure 7d).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of auditory selectivity in the unisensory training group.

claim: The unisensory training group did not exhibit population-level multisensory enhancement.
source: Furthermore, the unisensory training group did not exhibit population-level multisensory enhancement (n=174, Figure 7f).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of multisensory integration in the unisensory training group.

claim: The mean MSI for the A3k-VHz and A10k-VHz pairs in the unisensory training group showed no significant difference (p=0.327, paired t-test), with values of –0.02±0.12 and –0.01±0.13, respectively.
source: The mean MSI for the A3k-VHz and A10k-VHz pairs showed no significant difference (p=0.327, paired t-test), with values of –0.02±0.12 and –0.01±0.13, respectively (Figure 7g).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of MSI in the unisensory training group.

claim: Among audiovisual neurons in the unisensory training group, multisensory integration did not differ significantly between the two pairings (A3k-VHz vs A10k-VHz: 0.002±0.126 vs 0.017±0.147; p=0.63).
source: Even among audiovisual neurons (n=37), multisensory integration did not differ significantly between the two pairings (A3k-VHz vs A10k-VHz: 0.002±0.126 vs 0.017±0.147; p=0.63; Figure 7g).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison in audiovisual neurons from the unisensory training group.

claim: Most AC neurons exhibited distinct integrative patterns for different auditory-visual pairings, with multisensory enhancement observed primarily for favored pairings.
source: Our findings reveal that most AC neurons exhibited distinct integrative patterns for different auditory-visual pairings, with multisensory enhancement observed primarily for favored pairings.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings regarding integration patterns.

claim: AC neurons effectively discriminated between matched and mismatched auditory-visual pairings.
source: Furthermore, AC neurons effectively discriminated between matched and mismatched auditory-visual pairings, highlighting the crucial role of the AC in multisensory object recognition and discrimination.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings regarding discrimination abilities.

claim: A subset of auditory neurons developed visual responses and exhibited congruence between auditory and visual selectivity.
source: Interestingly, a subset of auditory neurons not only developed visual responses but also exhibited congruence between auditory and visual selectivity.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings regarding audiovisual neurons.

claim: Multisensory perceptual training establishes a memory trace of the trained audiovisual experiences within the AC.
source: These findings suggest that multisensory perceptual training establishes a memory trace of the trained audiovisual experiences within the AC and enhances the preferential linking of auditory and visual inputs.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed neural changes following training.

claim: Visual stimuli can modulate auditory responses in the AC via pathways involving the lateral posterior nucleus of the thalamus.
source: Studies have shown that visual stimuli can modulate auditory responses in the AC via pathways involving the lateral posterior nucleus of the thalamus (Chou et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The deep layers of the AC serve as crucial hubs for integrating cross-modal contextual information.
source: and the deep layers of the AC serve as crucial hubs for integrating cross-modal contextual information (Morrill et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Irrelevant visual cues can affect sound discrimination in AC.
source: Even irrelevant visual cues can affect sound discrimination in AC (Chang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There are reciprocal nerve projections between auditory and visual cortices.
source: Anatomical investigations reveal reciprocal nerve projections between auditory and visual cortices (Bizley et al., 2007; Stehberg et al., 2014; Falchier et al., 2002; Cappe and Barone, 2005; Campi et al., 2010; Banks et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: In the primary visual cortex, temporally congruent audiovisual stimuli elicit balanced enhancement and suppression, whereas incongruent stimuli predominantly result in suppression.
source: Moreover, two-photon calcium imaging in awake mice has shown that audiovisual encoding in the primary visual cortex depends on the temporal congruency of stimuli, with temporally congruent audiovisual stimuli eliciting balanced enhancement and suppression, whereas incongruent stimuli predominantly result in suppression (Meijer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a calcium imaging study.

claim: Sensory representations, including multisensory processing, are context-dependent.
source: However, sensory representations, including multisensory processing, are known to be context-dependent (Elgueda et al., 2019; Han et al., 2022; Otazu et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on context-dependent processing.

claim: Sensory representations can be shaped by perceptual learning.
source: and can be shaped by perceptual learning (Xu et al., 2014; Vincis and Fontanini, 2016; Knöpfel et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to perceptual learning studies.

claim: Multisensory cues facilitate decision-making.
source: This suggests that multisensory cues facilitate decision-making.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of behavioral performance data.

claim: Multisensory processing in the brain helps rats discriminate between cues more efficiently.
source: This indicates that multisensory processing in the brain helps rats discriminate between cues more efficiently
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of reaction time data.

claim: Actively engaging multiple senses is crucial for the benefits of multisensory integration.
source: suggesting that actively engaging multiple senses is crucial for the benefits of multisensory integration.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on comparison between task groups.

claim: Multisensory discrimination and subsequent behavioral reporting are necessary for biased enhancement.
source: indicating that multisensory discrimination and subsequent behavioral reporting are necessary for biased enhancement.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on comparison between task groups.

claim: Distinct integration models enhance cue selectivity in multisensory conditions.
source: This highlights how distinct integration models enhance cue selectivity in multisensory conditions.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the correlation between MSI difference and selectivity change.

claim: Consistent information across modalities strengthens multisensory integration.
source: This suggests that consistent information across modalities strengthens multisensory integration.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of differential integration for matched vs. unmatched cues.

claim: Associative learning experiences enabled AC neurons to develop multisensory discrimination abilities.
source: This suggests that associative learning experiences enabled AC neurons to develop multisensory discrimination abilities.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of decoding results for matched vs. unmatched cues.

claim: The preference for contralateral cues was not simply due to a general bias toward a specific cue, but rather reflected the specific associations the animals learned during training.
source: This strongly suggests that the preference was not simply due to a general bias toward a specific cue, but rather reflected the specific associations the animals learned during the training.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on comparison between left and right AC.

claim: AC neurons exhibit cue preference and biased multisensory enhancement based on the learned association between cues and behavioral choice.
source: These findings suggest that AC neurons exhibit cue preference and biased multisensory enhancement based on the learned association between cues and behavioral choice.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of findings from left AC recordings.

claim: The development of multisensory enhancement for specific audiovisual cues and the alignment of auditory and visual preferences likely depend on the association of auditory and visual stimuli with the corresponding behavioral choice during multisensory training.
source: These findings suggest that the development of multisensory enhancement for specific audiovisual cues and the alignment of auditory and visual preferences likely depend on the association of auditory and visual stimuli with the corresponding behavioral choice during multisensory training.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on comparison between multisensory and unisensory training groups.

claim: Unisensory training alone cannot replicate the effects of multisensory training.
source: Unisensory training alone cannot replicate these effects.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison between training groups.

claim: The multisensory perception reflected by behavioral choices (correct vs. incorrect) might be shaped by the underlying integration strength.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that the multisensory perception reflected by behavioral choices (correct vs. incorrect) might be shaped by the underlying integration strength.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the relationship between MSI and behavioral choice.

claim: Sensory cortices, like AC, may act as a vital bridge for communicating sensory information across different modalities.
source: Sensory cortices, like AC, may act as a vital bridge for communicating sensory information across different modalities.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Task-related differentially integrative patterns may not be exclusive to sensory cortices but could represent a general model in the brain.
source: We propose that task-related differentially integrative patterns may not be exclusive to sensory cortices but could represent a general model in the brain.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the findings.

claim: Associative learning may drive the formation of new connections between sensory and motor areas of the brain, such as cortico-cortical pathways.
source: Associative learning may drive the formation of new connections between sensory and motor areas of the brain, such as cortico-cortical pathways (Makino et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The synchronized auditory-visual selectivity may be a way for AC to bind corresponding auditory and visual features, potentially forming memory traces for learned multisensory objects.
source: This synchronized auditory-visual selectivity may be a way for AC to bind corresponding auditory and visual features, potentially forming memory traces for learned multisensory objects.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the observed selectivity patterns.

claim: Multisensory training could drive the formation of specialized neural circuits within the auditory cortex, facilitating integrated processing of related auditory and visual information.
source: These results indicate that multisensory training could drive the formation of specialized neural circuits within the auditory cortex, facilitating integrated processing of related auditory and visual information.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the training effects.

claim: The early timing of visual responses in AC indicates that the observed responses were less likely modulated by visually evoked body or orofacial movements.
source: This early timing indicates that the observed responses were less likely modulated by visually evoked body or orofacial movements, which typically occur with a delay relative to sensory cue onset (Oude Lohuis et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on response timing and citation to movement studies.

claim: Some of the audiovisual integration observed in the auditory cortex may represent a combination of multisensory processing and preparatory motor activity.
source: Consequently, some of the audiovisual integration observed in the auditory cortex may represent a combination of multisensory processing and preparatory motor activity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation acknowledging potential motor contributions.

claim: The strength of multisensory enhancement itself served as a key indicator in differentiating between matched and mismatched cues.
source: However, the strength of multisensory enhancement itself served as a key indicator in differentiating between matched and mismatched cues.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the role of MSI in cue discrimination.

claim: The nature of the semantic-like information plays a vital role in modifying multisensory integration at the neuronal level.
source: These findings provide compelling evidence that the nature of the semantic-like information plays a vital role in modifying multisensory integration at the neuronal level.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the effects of matched vs. mismatched cues.
